extracted.intended_audience: machine learning researchers, conference organizers, reviewers, area chairs, and developers of AI-assisted peer-review tools
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for producing and assessing peer reviews (and AI tools that assist them) in machine-learning conference workflows, including reviewer form items, review-quality dimensions, AC decision-support, author rebuttal practices, and dataset requirements for building AI assistants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideal reviewer — Comprehensive Knowledge Base
rubrics_metrics.description: An 'ideal' reviewer possesses a Comprehensive Knowledge Base encompassing all relevant prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As part of the 'ideal' reviewer conceptualization (Section 4.2), the reviewer should be aware of relevant prior work to properly situate contributions and identify missing citations or incorrect novelty claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideal reviewer — Meticulous Verifiability
rubrics_metrics.description: An 'ideal' reviewer demonstrates Meticulous Verifiability to check claims and experimental setups with high accuracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This includes checking methodological details, ensuring claims are supported by evidence, and verifying reproducibility-related aspects where possible (Section 4.2). AI tools (RAV, code analysis) can assist but human judgment remains central.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideal reviewer — Insightful Constructivism
rubrics_metrics.description: An 'ideal' reviewer provides Insightful Constructivism: perfectly targeted, actionable feedback that maximally improves the paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Feedback should be concrete and aimed at helping authors improve their work rather than merely rejecting it (Section 4.2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Coverage of key evaluation criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviews should touch on core dimensions: novelty/originality, significance/impact, technical soundness/quality, empirical validation/reproducibility, clarity, and ethical considerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From the REVIEW_GUIDELINES: 'Please touch on the following dimensions: Quality (technical soundness), Clarity, Significance, Originality.' Reviewers should ensure coverage of these essential paper aspects and mention missing dimensions when absent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specificity of criticisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticisms should be concrete and actionable rather than vague or generic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper repeatedly emphasizes that a good review's weaknesses should be specific (e.g., not just 'needs more experiments' but which experiments, on which datasets, or against which baselines). The Review Report Card explicitly assesses Specificity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence base for review claims / factual rigor
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims made in a review should be backed by evidence or grounded references; reviewers should avoid unsupported assertions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: AI-assisted RAV (Retrieval Augmented Verification) can help cross-reference claims to literature. The automated report-card and guidance encourage cross-checking assertions (e.g., pointing to exact sections or theorems) and flagging when evidence is missing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructiveness and tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviews should be constructive in spirit and professional in tone, aimed at improving the work rather than dismissing authors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Review Guidelines and Report Card ask reviewers to maintain a professional, respectful tone and to phrase critiques to help authors revise (the Report Card notes 'Maintains a constructive, collegial tone').

rubrics_metrics.name: Summary (reviewer's own words)
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide a brief summary of the paper and its contributions in your own words; this section is not for critique or pasting the abstract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From the REVIEW_GUIDELINES: 'This is not the place to critique the paper... please provide the summary in your own understanding after reading.' A well-written summary helps ensure reviewer comprehension and agreement with basic claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strengths and Weaknesses (thorough assessment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide a thorough assessment of the paper's strengths and weaknesses, framed as reasons one might accept or reject the paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A good framing is to list concrete reasons to accept/reject and to touch on dimensions like novelty, significance, technical soundness, evaluation, and clarity. The guidelines encourage reviewers to think of 'reasons you might accept or reject the paper.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality rating (4-point scale)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assign a numerical rating for 'Quality' on a 1 (poor)–4 (excellent) scale reflecting technical soundness, appropriateness of methods, and rigor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The review form instructs: 'Based on what you discussed in Strengths and Weaknesses please assign the paper a numerical rating' with 4=excellent, 3=good, 2=fair, 1=poor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity rating (4-point scale)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assign a numerical rating for 'Clarity' on a 1–4 scale indicating how well the paper is written and organized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarity rating is to be based on the Strengths and Weaknesses assessment; a well-organized and informative paper should score higher and include constructive suggestions if clarity is lacking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significance rating (4-point scale)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assign a numerical rating for 'Significance' on a 1–4 scale measuring impact and likely uptake by the community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether others will build on the idea, if it advances understanding, or provides unique data or conclusions; map to 4=excellent impact down to 1=poor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality rating (4-point scale)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assign a numerical rating for 'Originality' on a 1–4 scale reflecting novelty and how the work differs from prior contributions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Originality can include novel combinations of techniques or new insights from evaluation; reviewers should cite relevant prior work when questioning novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overall score (10-point accept/reject scale)
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide an overall categorical score (1–10) mapping to Accept/Reject judgments with detailed descriptors (10 Strong Accept ... 1 Desk Reject).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The review form provides explicit textual definitions for each choice (10 Strong Accept: Technical flawless with groundbreaking impact; 1 Desk Reject: Not suitable for review due to major violations). Use these descriptions to choose the overall decision category.

rubrics_metrics.name: Questions (actionable list & criteria for score change)
rubrics_metrics.description: List and carefully describe ~3–5 actionable questions or suggestions that could change your opinion; explicitly state criteria under which the evaluation score could increase or decrease.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From the REVIEW_GUIDELINES: 'Think of the things where a response from the author can change your opinion... You are strongly encouraged to state the clear criteria under which your evaluation score could increase or decrease.' This makes rebuttal phases more productive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations and negative societal impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the authors have adequately addressed limitations and potential negative societal impacts; reward transparency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If authors have been upfront about limitations or risks, a simple 'yes' may suffice; otherwise provide constructive suggestions. The guidelines emphasize rewarding authors for acknowledging limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidence score (1–5)
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide a confidence score (1–5) indicating how certain you are in your assessment and your familiarity with related work and details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The form gives descriptions for each confidence level (5 = absolutely certain; 1 = educated guess / outside your area). Use this to communicate reliability of your assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Automated Review 'Report Card' dimensions
rubrics_metrics.description: An AI-produced 'Report Card' assesses a human review on multiple dimensions: Coverage (key aspects addressed), Specificity (concrete/actionable), Constructiveness, and Tone; often presented on a 1–5 scale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Coverage of essential paper aspects (novelty, significance, soundness), Specificity of critiques, Evidence backing claims (cross-checked with RAV), and Constructiveness/Tone.' Report cards can be released before/after rebuttal to nudge reviewer behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retrieval Augmented Verification (RAV) and Grounding
rubrics_metrics.description: AI systems should ground claims by connecting LLM outputs to authoritative knowledge bases (e.g., Semantic Scholar, arXiv) to cross-reference claims and suggest relevant citations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: RAV enables AI to explain why a retrieved document supports/refutes a claim and to flag missed citations; it is foundational for factual rigor but depends on access to literature and reliable retrieval.

rubrics_metrics.name: AI for Code Analysis and Reproducibility Assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: AI tools should parse methodology and analyze provided source code to identify errors, missing dependencies, data leakage, or mismatches between code and paper descriptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such tools can perform 'sanity checks', identify common pitfalls, and support preliminary reproducibility assessment; conferences are encouraged to encourage code submission to enable this analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: AI for Content Provenance and Authenticity
rubrics_metrics.description: Use methods (e.g., watermarking like SynthID, statistical textual features such as perplexity/burstiness) to detect AI-generated text as one signal among many, acknowledging limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper warns these methods have high false-positive rates, fairness concerns, and can be bypassed; detectors should be contextualized and not used as sole arbiter of provenance. The latent intent and nature of AI contribution matter more than a raw detector score.

rubrics_metrics.name: AI-Assisted Authoring Support (pre-submission simulated review)
rubrics_metrics.description: LLMs can provide formative pre-submission feedback: clarity, structure, argument coherence, completeness of literature review, adherence to ethical/reporting guidelines, and a 'simulated review' prioritizing potential weaknesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: AI can simulate multiple reviewer personas (theory-focused, application-focused) and suggest concrete actionables (e.g., 'consider adding an ablation study for parameter X' or 'link Section 2 to Section 3'). This is framed as formative, not authoritative.

rubrics_metrics.name: AI-Assisted Rebuttal Support
rubrics_metrics.description: Tools should systematically catalog significant reviewer points, ensure each is addressed in rebuttals, suggest how to present new evidence, and help authors judge adequacy of responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: AI can help distinguish misunderstanding from substantive disagreement and recommend which points may change reviewer opinions; RAV and code-analysis agents can validate reviewer claims where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: AI Decision Support for Area Chairs (meta-review assistance)
rubrics_metrics.description: AI should synthesize multiple reviews and rebuttals, summarize key arguments, highlight consensus/disagreement and unaddressed concerns, and assist in drafting meta-reviews while leaving final judgment to the AC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Capabilities include conflict highlighting (e.g., Reviewer 1 praises novelty while Reviewer 2 calls it incremental), flagging reviews with poor evidence/tone, and producing concise overviews to guide AC deliberation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data requirement: Structured reviewer reasoning for score changes and key assertions
rubrics_metrics.description: Datasets for AI assistants must capture explicit, structured reviewer reasoning explaining why scores changed (or not) and link reasoning to specific rebuttal points or discussion elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper argues this is essential for training models to predict score changes or to understand deliberation; coarse signals (final scores only) are insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data requirement: Detailed author–reviewer–AC interaction traces with semantic annotations
rubrics_metrics.description: Collect dialogue acts (clarification, concession), argument strength, and explicit response chains with semantic annotations linking interactions across the review lifecycle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These traces enable modeling negotiation, clarification dynamics, and deliberation quality; collection must balance burden, privacy/anonymity, and anti-gaming.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data requirement: AC deliberation traces (anonymized & aggregated)
rubrics_metrics.description: Capture how Area Chairs weigh conflicting reviews, assess rebuttals, identify decision drivers, and form meta-review judgments in an anonymized and aggregated form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such traces help train decision-support systems and understand human weighting strategies while preserving privacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data requirement: Fine-grained annotations linking review statements to manuscript and external knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Annotate links from review statements to specific manuscript parts (sentences, figures) and to external prior work/theories to improve traceability and grounding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These annotations support claim-level verification, enable RAV to justify flagged issues, and improve interpretability of automated suggestions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation metrics for LLM-assisted review tasks
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure performance of LLMs on review-generation and rating tasks using metrics like Recall for extracted strengths/weaknesses/rebuttal points and MAE/RMSE for rating prediction (plus direction/magnitude of score change).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The illustrative experiments use Recall (Avg Hits / Avg Real Points) for component extraction and MAE/RMSE for rating prediction, noting that predicting exact score changes is hard and direction/magnitude may be more informative.
